_note: Viewing pass over the 84 Hans Erik Lund candidates for Copenhagen's 26 new trees. Every file below was downloaded and LOOKED at. Licence for anything approved: 'Used with permission from Hans Erik Lund, Dansk Dendrologisk Forening; credit required', attribution 'Hans Erik Lund'.

verdicts.reason: The whole hawthorn on its grass bank, in leaf, a man beside the trunk for scale: crown and trunk both readable, tree dead centre, daylight colour. Leaves in the sibling frame are shallow broad-lobed Crataegus with a haw, and the low twisted multi-limbed frame and 2.2m trunk match the record.
A fine study of the twisted limbs and root flare, but the crown is cut off entirely: a trunk close-up, not a portrait.
Leaf spray close-up. Useful as species proof (lobed Crataegus leaves, one haw) and nothing a card can show.
Trunk only, filling the frame from bark to bark; no crown, no tree.

The whole oak standing free on the deer-park grass, in leaf against blue sky, its huge burred base visible at the foot: crown and trunk both readable and centred. Oak habit and foliage; the low wide bole matches an 8.9m girth, and the crown is taller and more irregular than Kuppelegen's dome 100m away, so the two frames are clearly two trees.
Not a Hans Erik Lund photograph: the register filename credits GT, so it falls outside the permission we hold and cannot be published whatever it shows.

The whole maple bare in March, blue sky, people at its foot for scale, the sawn-off major limbs the register describes plainly visible. A bare veteran whose architecture is the argument, which is the standard's own exception; trunk and crown both readable and dead centre. Species not confirmable from leaves in March, but the corky finely fissured pale bark in the next frame (shot a minute later, same tree) is field maple, and the register knows its own third-thickest navr.
Base of the same tree from underneath: good corky field-maple bark, no crown.

The whole oak in leaf, sunlit under blue sky, its broad dome filling the frame and the thick bole clear at the base. Pedunculate oak in the deer park, and the crown is the flat wide dome its name claims, plainly a different tree from Trepileegen's taller frame.
Lichen-covered trunk base filling the frame. No crown.
Trunk study: the warty bole from ground to first limbs, crown cut away.
Shot from directly beneath, looking up the trunk into the branches. Oak leaves confirm the species and the tree has no readable shape.

Composition meets the standard: the whole oak alone on the grassland, in leaf, trunk and crown readable and centred. Held because photo_light calls it POOR on a blown white sky, and that reading looks wrong to me: this is flat overcast, not backlit, and the tree keeps its colour and detail rather than going to silhouette. Worth a second opinion before it ships or dies.
Another trunk study, the warts and burrs beautifully shown and the crown absent.
The multi-stemmed base among leaf litter, houses behind, crown cut off. Grey winter light.
The same stems from a little further back; still a base study, still no crown.

The whole hornbeam, bare, on a flat grey day against a white sky with apartment blocks behind it. Reads dormant and nearly colourless, and a hornbeam's bare frame is not the architecture the winter exception was written for.

The whole oak bare on the deer-park grass beside its snow-dusted barrow: heavy crooked low limbs, the hollowed base, crown and trunk both readable and centred. A veteran whose frame is the point, which is the standard's winter exception, and the burnt hollow in the next frame of the same session confirms the tree.
Trunk study showing the burnt hollow at the base. Confirms which oak this is, shows no tree.

The lime from the garden path, bare in early spring under blue sky: trunk fully readable, most of the crown in frame, tree centred with the garden and the old brewery buildings behind. Bare, so the silver undersides cannot be seen, but the fine pendulous branchlets of a weeping lime show in the sibling frames of the same run, and the wires holding the main limbs are there as the register describes.
Trunk and lower limbs only, from underneath. No crown.
Looking straight up into the branches at the bracing wires. Documents the wires, shows no tree.

Whole tree from the other side, and badly backlit against a white sky with an apartment block behind: washed out and nearly colourless. It does show the weeping branchlets, which is why the species reads.

The whole maple on the park lawn, bare in November on a flat grey day, tree centred and dominant with the trunk cluster readable from the ground up. Multi-stemmed from about a metre exactly as the register says, pale finely fissured corky bark on the stems in the sibling frames: field maple. Bare and dull-lit, but it is the best of four and a bare frame beats no frame.
The stems from close in, crown cut off at the top of the frame.
Same again from another side: base and stems, no crown.
Whole tree from the road side, but a block of flats fills the frame behind it and the tree sits smaller. The other whole-tree frame is cleaner.

The whole beech against the National Gallery's white gable, bare on a grey February day, its low layering limbs sweeping out to the right. Tree centred, trunk and crown both readable, and the building says exactly where to stand. Flat light and the gable takes the left third, which is the honest weakness; it is the only whole-tree frame of four and a bare photograph beats none.
Trunk with the sawn-off branch stubs, almost colourless. Confirms smooth grey beech bark, shows no tree.
The layering limbs rooting into the leaf litter beside the path: a detail, and no crown or trunk.
Close study of the bole and its cut stubs, carved with initials. Not a portrait.

The whole Oriental plane on its round lawn, bare in spring under blue sky, the honorary residence to the right exactly where the record puts it twenty metres off. Tree centred, trunk and crown both readable, mottled flaking plane bark plain on the bole and the very uneven lower trunk the register notes clearly there. Plane beyond doubt from the bark and the fruit balls; the low wide sinuous crown reads Oriental rather than London.

Closer study of the same plane, the burred lumpy bole with the mansion and its statues behind and the fruit balls hanging in the limbs. Crown top is cut, so it is not a lead, but it shows the thing the wide frame cannot.
The elephant-foot root flare the register describes, filling the frame. A detail, not a tree.
The whole beech, but shot late on a dull winter afternoon: the tree is a dark tangle against a grey sky, the trunk is behind a hedge and the sun is going down at the right. Daylight in name only.
Trunk and radiating limbs from close in, crown cut off at the top, flat grey light.
Leaning trunk and lower limbs against the church wall, in leaf, crown cut off at the top. Confirms the pinnate leaves and the furrowed bark; not a portrait.
Same tree, same day, framed on the trunk against the brick gable with the crown running out of the top of the frame.

The whole pagoda tree in full summer leaf beside Sankt Thomas Kirke, exactly where the record puts it: crown complete, trunk clear at the base, tree centred and dominant with the red-brick church anchoring the left edge. Pinnate leaves and the dense regrown crown of a tree cut back hard, as the register describes.
Flat and almost colourless by the meter, no separation between tree and background.
Bark close-up showing the damage on the lower trunk. Explicitly outside the standard.

The hollowed, deeply ridged bole with pinnate wingnut foliage hanging around it and a bench behind. No crown, so not a lead, but it is the thing the wide frame cannot show and it confirms the species.

The whole wingnut in full summer leaf in the Allegade park, centred and dominant, crown complete and dense, with the street, a bus and the flowerbed placing it. White blown sky is the weakness and the tree itself is well lit and green; the trunk sits in its own shade, which the trunk frame beside it answers.

The whole plane in leaf on the lawn behind the old auditorium, a person and a dog at its foot for scale: crown complete, bole readable from the ground with the mottled flaking plane bark on it, tree centred against the long yellow-brick building the record names. Blue sky, good light.
Shot from underneath into the canopy: several stems and leaves, no tree shape and no ground.
Root flare and the base of two stems with three visitors standing in front. The people take the frame and there is no crown.
Close-up of the bracket fungus in a crevice. Records the decay the register notes, shows no tree.
Photograph of the garden's own label screwed to the trunk, reading Zelkova serrata. Settles the species beyond argument and is not a picture of a tree.
Close study of the root plate spreading over bare soil. A detail.
The four-stemmed base and roots from a few metres back, beautifully lit, crown entirely out of frame.
Trunk study on the pavement, mottled plane bark filling the frame, no crown.

A boy with his arms round the trunk: it gives the girth a scale nothing else here does, and the crown is absent so it could only ever be a second picture. Held rather than used because the subject is an identifiable child on a public pavement, which is not my call to publish.

The whole plane in full leaf towering over the street corner, crown complete to the top of the frame and the pale trunk readable at the foot, with the red-brick block on the left placing it. In leaf, sunlit, tree dominant; the building takes the left third, which is what a street tree's portrait looks like.
Bark close-up with red graffiti on it. Outside the standard twice over.

The whole cottonwood in full summer leaf on the chapel lawn, trunk readable from the grass up and the crown complete against a bright sky. The leaf frames from the same run show the long-pointed finely toothed leaves of Populus acuminata. Worth saying plainly: the register entry is a group of three and the measurements belong to the northernmost, so this is the stand our page is about rather than a proven single trunk.
Leaf spray close-up. Confirms the species and shows no tree.
Leaves against grass, close up. Species evidence, not a photograph of a tree.
Another leaf close-up from the same run.

The whole catalpa in fresh leaf against a blue sky with cloud, centred and filling the frame, forking at about two metres exactly as the register says. Big heart-shaped leaves and the open airy crown of Catalpa bignonioides, and the garden's own label in the next frame names the species on this trunk. The hedge screens the lowest metre of the bole.
The fork and lower limbs from close in, crown cut off at the top.
The garden's label on the trunk: Catalpa bignonioides. Species proof, not a tree photograph.

The whole tulip tree bare against a clear blue sky on the garden's western lawn, trunk readable from the grass to the first fork and the crown complete. Bare, so no tulip leaves, but the trunk frame from the same minute shows the fine diamond-lattice bark of Liriodendron, and it is the one tulip tree in this garden.
The bole to the first fork, good diamond-patterned bark, crown out of frame.

The same oak from the gatehouse side, in autumn leaf with the red Fortunporthuset beside it: the frame that tells you where to stand. Tree sits left of centre and the sky is blown white, so it is the second picture rather than the lead.

The whole oak in autumn leaf standing clear on the deer-park ground, dead centre, trunk readable from its ring of boulders up and the wide crown complete. Soft overcast light and the colour holds. The asymmetric crown the register notes reads here too.
The base, the root plate and the boundary stone from close in, with the beeches behind. A detail.
The only candidate for this tree, and it is a trunk study: deeply ridged rope-like Robinia bark filling the frame, crown entirely absent.
The avenue from across the lawn, small in a wide panoramic frame under a grey sky. A distant view: you have to look for the blossom.

The cherries in full blossom filling the frame from the lawn, trunks and crowns both readable, visitors small underneath for scale. The ensemble is the destination here and it is unmistakably the subject; pale pink semi-double flowers on bare wood in late April, which is Accolade. Grey sky at the top edge is the weakness.

The avenue from inside, a tunnel of blossom over the path with people walking through it: the thing the avenue is famous for, which the wide frame cannot say. Grey light washes the pink, so it is the second picture.
The same tunnel with a crowd filling the lower half of the frame, many faces close and identifiable. The blossom is good and the people are the picture.

The whole oak bare in the cemetery, but shot into a blown white sky: pale, low contrast and drained of colour, which is exactly what the exposure rule is for. Bare, so nothing shows the Caucasian oak either.
The grafted base smothered in burr growth, which is the swelling the register says takes the girth to about four metres. Good evidence, no crown.
The tree stands centre-left with a big conifer taking the left third and another bare crown tangled into it from the right. You have to work out which trunk is meant.
Trunk and fork from close in, blue sky, crown running out of the top of the frame.

The whole service tree bare against a clear blue sky, centred, trunk readable from the grass and the crown complete above it. Bare, so no leaves or fruit; the scaly plated bark in the sibling frame fits Sorbus domestica and it is the one service tree in this garden. A modest portrait rather than a striking one, and it is honest and it is the tree.
Trunk in summer leaf, bark filling the frame, crown cut off.
Second whole-tree frame in leaf, closer in, but the crown runs into the foliage of the trees behind it at the top. The clean one beside it is better.

From under the canopy: the trunk rising out of the lawn into the whole radiating limb structure, dead centre, summer green. Crown outline is cut, so not a lead, and it shows the frame of the tree that the wide shot flattens.

The whole oak in full summer leaf, free-standing and full-crowned on the cemetery lawn, which is word for word what the register says of it. Dead centre, crown complete, trunk readable to the ground. Blown white sky is the weakness and the tree is richly green and correctly exposed.
Wider view with the honorary residence taking the right half and the plane pushed to the left edge. Good for the setting, wrong shape for a card.
Street view with the tree behind a scaffold pole, road signs, parked cars and the church. Cluttered; the tree has to be picked out.
From underneath the canopy: the fork and the leaves overhead, crown outline gone and the frame closed in by a hedge. Not a portrait.
Leaves and the long hanging bean pods, close up. Settles the species beyond doubt and shows no tree.
